extracted.intended_audience: journalists, public-relations professionals, and media-studies students
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or composing press releases to maximize pickup by news media using Galtung & Ruge's 1965 news values (and later updates). Focuses on which event attributes make a story more likely to be selected by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more factors an event satisfies, the higher the probability it becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galtung & Ruge propose that newsworthiness accumulates: items that meet multiple news factors are increasingly likely to be selected. Use this as a heuristic that combining several values in a release strengthens pickup odds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The factors will tend to exclude each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some news values are mutually exclusive or operate in trade-off: emphasizing one attribute may reduce another (e.g., routine frequency vs. unexpectedness). Be aware of tensions when crafting framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion (of low-factor events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events satisfying none or few factors will not become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a release fails to hit any significant news values, editors are unlikely to cover it. Releases should aim to satisfy at least one strong factor or several weaker ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that happen quickly fit news cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, timely events that align with the news rhythm are favored; time-sensitivity increases editorial interest. For releases, tie items to current windows or deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger events more likely covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude/scale matters: bigger consequences, larger numbers, or higher stakes pass the threshold for newsworthiness. For PR, emphasize scale or wider impact to cross editors' thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, simple events preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that are easy to interpret and describe are more likely to be chosen. Press releases should use unambiguous language and simple narratives to aid rapid editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural relevance to audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that resonate with the target audience's cultural frames or experiences are prioritized. Tailor releases to the cultural context of the publication’s readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fits expectations of audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items that match existing expectations, stereotypes, or newsroom schemas are more easily recognized as news. Align framing with familiar angles where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprising events preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel or counter-intuitive elements increase interest. Press releases gain traction when they highlight surprises or developments that defy expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a story is news, it stays news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing storylines generate follow-ups and sustained coverage. Frame releases as sequels, updates, or part of an ongoing narrative to exploit continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mix of news in publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consider the balance of content across an edition; a release may be chosen to fill a desired mix. Understand an outlet’s composition to position your release appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories referencing elite countries are more newsworthy (cultural factor for Western press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International status matters: linkage to powerful countries increases pickup chances for Western media. For PR, foreground international or elite-country relevance where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite people
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving elite or prominent people are more newsworthy (cultural factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name recognition and status boost interest. Mention prominent organizations or figures in the release to raise editorial attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with an individual focus are preferred (human-interest angle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on individuals makes abstract events more relatable. Use personal stories, spokespeople, or profiles to increase a release’s appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news is more newsworthy than good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict, risk, loss, or scandal attract coverage more readily than neutral or positive items. Highlight risks, problems, or stakes when ethically and strategically appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-release pickup factors (explicit application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases are more likely to be picked up if they reference elite institutions/people, have a clear individual or company at the center, contain negativity/conflict/risk, are unexpected, fit cultural narratives, have continuing storylines, have clarity, and cross threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This application list translates Galtung & Ruge into PR practice: ensure your release names prominent actors, presents an unambiguous narrative centered on a person/org, emphasizes surprise or conflict if present, ties to cultural frames, signals follow-ups, and states scale/impact. Use these points as a checklist when drafting releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: The power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving powerful political or economic elites are newsworthy (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001 update).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to 'reference to elite people/nations' but updated for contemporary elite actors; emphasize connections to institutional power in releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrity involvement increases newsworthiness (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrity names or endorsement can raise pickup chances, especially in outlets oriented to popular culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment value is a news factor (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with entertainment appeal (humor, spectacle, drama) can be prioritized; tailor releases for lifestyle/entertainment desks where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprising events remain a key value (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces Galtung & Ruge’s unexpectedness; craft releases to foreground novel or unexpected angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news continues to attract coverage (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize problems, conflicts, or negative outcomes when ethically appropriate to increase news interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive developments can also be newsworthy (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include good-news angles—innovation, success, benefits—especially for outlets that cover constructive or solutions journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale or magnitude matters (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates threshold: emphasize numbers, reach, or impact in releases to convey significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance to the audience is central (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor releases to demonstrate direct relevance to an outlet’s readership or locale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential for follow-up stories increases value (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal future developments, timelines, or ongoing investigations to encourage editorial commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern update: Newspaper agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Alignment with an outlet’s agenda or editorial priorities influences selection (Harcup & O'Neill, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch releases that match a target publication’s stated beats, campaigns, or thematic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit press-release rubric (Galtung–Ruge synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release is more newsworthy if it concerns a prominent person/org, has a clear simple narrative, has surprise, cultural relevance, emotional pull (negativity/human story), crosses size/scale threshold, and has follow-up potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implicit checklist synthesizes the theory into PR-focused advice: include prominence, clarity, surprise or emotional hooks, scale, cultural hooks, and sequel potential when possible. Use as a compact practical rubric when editing drafts.
